pack-0001.title: Field reading together
pack-0001.quote: In everything, appearance and essence are in contradiction. …Otherwise, if intuition alone could reveal the essence, what would science be for? What would research be for?

sections.body:
In everything, appearance and essence are in contradiction. …Otherwise, if intuition alone could reveal the essence, what would science be for? What would research be for?

Mao Zedong's Speech at the National Conference of the Communist Party of China, 1955-03-31. Mao Zedong's Collected Works, Volume 6, page 401, People’s Publishing House, 1999 edition.

These two sentences appear in Part III of the meeting’s concluding speech. The speech explains the role of scientific research through the relationship between studying appearances and understanding essence.

On March 31, 1955, Mao Zedong delivered concluding remarks at the CPC National Conference. Following discussion of the Gao Gang and Rao Shushi affair, this passage considers why appearances can mislead and how judgments should rest on actual evidence.

If you are worried about work, speak to two people in similar roles. Ask what they did less of, and more of, last month. If both mention more review work, try reviewing an old project yourself. You do not need to decide the future of your career tonight; find one useful thing to do tomorrow.

Working through it together reveals whether they need an example, access permissions, or reassurance that questions are welcome.

Ask, “Could you take me through it from the beginning?” Watching someone work around a fault teaches what the instructions leave out. After offering advice, ask that person which step you have overlooked.

It's okay to clean up only one place today. For example, put away the things you need tomorrow morning. Such little things in life will leave clarity and initiative to the next day, and also let you know that change can start from a small step.

These small actions will cause less trouble until tomorrow. The clarity of life can also be accumulated by tidying up little by little, and there is no need to always wait for a big change.

pack-0361.title: All kinds of experiences should be learned.
pack-0361.quote: Learn from different kinds of experience; do not apply one template everywhere.

sections.body:
Two Talks on Agricultural Mutual Assistance and Cooperation (October 15, November 4, 1953)

Collected Works of Mao Zedong, Volume 6, People’s Publishing House, page 300

Learn from different kinds of experience; do not apply one template everywhere.
In autumn 1953, Mao twice discussed agricultural mutual aid and cooperation, including the organization of mutual-aid teams and cooperatives and lessons from pilot projects.

One method is effective in large teams, and small teams may not be able to afford it. One person's recovery method may not be suitable for another family's arrangement. Put the same method in different conditions for comparison.

The method shared by others can ask him to explain where he lives, what support he has, and how to arrange his time. Borrow more under similar conditions, and try different places by yourself. Judgment grows slowly after comparison.

After absorbing a variety of experiences, choose the part that suits you. Being able to explain where the difference comes from is better to cope with change than to remember a universal template.

pack-0362.title: If you are not ready, you'd rather push it.
pack-0362.quote: If preparations are incomplete, it is better to postpone.

sections.body:
"If the preparation for the operation of Dinghai is not postponed" (November 14, 1949)

Military Science Publishing House and Central Party Literature Press, Mao Zedong's Military Anthology, Volume 6, sent to Su Yu on November 14, 1949 and told Chen Yi and Rao Shushi.

If preparations are incomplete, it is better to postpone.

This sentence gives specific instructions for preparing the operation against Dinghai.

In November 1949, the People’s Liberation Army planned operations against Zhoushan. In a November 14 telegram to Su Yu and others, Mao called for rechecking troop strength, deployment, preparation, and timing.

The key preparations have not been made yet, and the postponement can avoid forcing the risk to everyone. Make a specific statement about the gap, and make a new appointment to complete the conditions and review the date.

The sooner the news of the postponement is announced, the more relevant people can arrange it. Give the conditions that really need to be made up, and then agree on the confirmation time. The new date should be on the action that has already begun.

The time has been delayed, and the action is still going on. As long as you know what to rely on next time to increase your confidence, you will have a clear purpose in the future.

pack-0363.title: Don't fight unprepared battles, don't fight
pack-0363.quote: Fight no battle without preparation or confidence in victory.

sections.body:
Strategy for the Second Year of the War of Liberation (September 1, 1947)

Selected Collections of Mao Zedong, Volume 4, People’s Publishing House, 2nd Edition, 1991, page 1233

Fight no battle without preparation or confidence in victory.
In September 1947, the civil war entered its second year. Mao drafted Central Committee instructions clarifying strategic offensive deployments and the tasks of different units.

When making an important decision, list the minimum conditions and the methods that can be withdrawn. If you are enthusiastic but not prepared enough, you must first make up a basic condition. There is a lot of preparation but there is still a lack of key evidence. You can change the path.

The decision that is really difficult to withdraw can be prepared to a sober person and ask him to point out which one is just his own hope. If there is still a gap, do a little test, and then decide whether to work harder.

Courage can be used to face the possible consequences seriously. It is necessary to judge whether to move forward with a grasp or reserve a more suitable opportunity for the future.

pack-0364.title: Two poems of Lu Xun, "Hongmei
pack-0364.quote: Lu Xun’s two lines—“With a cold brow I face a thousand pointing fingers; with bowed head I willingly serve the children as an ox”—should become our motto.

sections.body:
Talks at the Yenan Forum on Literature and Art (May 1942)

Selected Works of Mao Zedong, Volume 3, People’s Publishing House, 1991, 2nd Edition, Page 877

Lu Xun’s two lines—“With a cold brow I face a thousand pointing fingers; with bowed head I willingly serve the children as an ox”—should become our motto.

The two lines come from Lu Xun’s poem Self-Mockery. Mao Zedong quotes them within his concluding speech.
In May 1942, the Yan’an Forum on Literature and Art discussed intended audiences, artistic creation, and evaluation during the war. The text consists of the May 2 introduction and May 23 conclusion.

When the voice is noisy, judging whose evaluation is worth taking time to respond to, and who is just an onlooker. At the same time, see which person around you really needs help.

It can be quiet to help others. Write the process of one investigation to the next person, or explain the problem for the person in trouble. If you know where you should spend your strength, you will be less led away by onlookers.

You can give some time, teach a movement, or reduce the trouble for others. Where the power is used, it will gradually become your true position.

pack-0365.title: For the sake of sacrifice and ambition, dare to teach
pack-0365.quote: Sacrifice strengthens our resolve; we dare to make the sun and moon shine on a new world.

sections.body:
Seven Laws · To Shaoshan (June 1959)

"Mao Zedong's Poems" of the Central Party Literature Press, neck couplet; the text refers to the interpretation of the Communist Party of China News Network.

Sacrifice strengthens our resolve; we dare to make the sun and moon shine on a new world.

This is the neck couplet of the whole poem.
In June 1959, Mao returned to Shaoshan, Hunan, recalling his departure in youth and local revolutionary history. The poem links a personal homecoming with social change.

If you want to change a set of stubborn practices, first choose a visible link and find people who are willing to work together to try new results. Set the scope of the necessary costs, and also take care of those who are willing to bear it together.

For example, if you want to improve the traffic of an old community, you can first mark the places that are most prone to tripping with residents, discuss where to change first, and then look back to see if it is convenient for the elderly to walk. The change will remain in the people who pass by later.

The results leave the process and methods, so that later generations can take over. Far-reaching changes grow from the small part of reality, and the efforts that can be passed on will not stop on this day.
